title: HTTP Request Smuggling

source_subtopics.title: Coordinated testing of HTTP protocol handling

subtopics: Coordinated testing of HTTP protocol handling
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in HTTP Request Smuggling.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for HTTP Request Smuggling and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for HTTP Request Smuggling, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 13: SSRF, Request Routing, and HTTP Infrastructure Attacks. It builds practical understanding of HTTP Request Smuggling with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: HTTP Request Smuggling addresses how untrusted data or requests cross a boundary and may influence application behavior. The safe fix should address the root cause and remain testable. Make proxy/application behavior consistent, avoid trust in caller-controlled headers, separate private from shared responses, and test the deployed configuration with controlled evidence.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: HTTP Request Smuggling can be understood through this sequence: Inspect request/response → Identify boundary mismatch → Apply narrow control → Test deployment behavior. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 95.1 Frontend and backend HTTP parsing; 95.2 Reverse proxies and application servers; 95.3 Conflicting message-length interpretation; 95.4 HTTP request desynchronization concepts; 95.5 Secure proxy and server configuration; 95.6 Coordinated testing of HTTP protocol handling. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Make proxy/application behavior consistent, avoid trust in caller-controlled headers, separate private from shared responses, and test the deployed configuration with controlled evidence.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: HTTP Request Smuggling
content_blocks.code:
GET /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.test
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: no-store
content_blocks.expected_output: The response declares JSON content and asks caches not to retain this personalized response.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This is a schematic transcript for a local test app. Confirm actual headers in the browser network panel or an authorized HTTP client.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Make proxy/application behavior consistent, avoid trust in caller-controlled headers, separate private from shared responses, and test the deployed configuration with controlled evidence. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “HTTP Request Smuggling”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for HTTP Request Smuggling in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: HTTP Request Smuggling is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Make proxy/application behavior consistent, avoid trust in caller-controlled headers, separate private from shared responses, and test the deployed configuration with controlled evidence.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
